planting.note: Plant tuber sections or root crowns in spring once soil is workable, in deep, loose, well-drained ground free of rocks so the long, brittle taproot can descend straight down.

directions: Plant tuber sections or nursery root crowns in spring at the edge of woodland plantings or against a sturdy trellis, since the twining vines climb 8-12 feet and the deeply descending tubers need loose, loamy ground to form straight roots. Dioscorea japonica, the source of Japan's prized jinenjo, naturally grows along forest margins and thickets and tolerates filtered woodland shade, though tuber size is largest with at least a half-day of sun. Harvest the mucilaginous white tubers in late fall after the heart-shaped leaves yellow and die back, digging carefully since roots can descend two feet or more; grate the raw tuber into the classic tororo topping for soba noodles or rice. Leave a few finger-sized root sections or the small aerial bulbils that form in leaf axils in the ground to replant the following spring.

planting.note: Direct sow or set out divisions in spring in moderately fertile, humus-rich soil beneath high-canopy trees or along a woodland edge; the clump establishes within its first season.

directions: Sow seed in spring in moderately fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade beneath high-canopy trees or along a woodland edge; germination is quick and the clump-forming perennial establishes within its first season. Once rooted, Fagopyrum dibotrys sends up a steady flush of lemony-flavored young leaves and tender stem tips that can be picked repeatedly through the growing season and used raw in salads or wilted into cooked greens much like spinach. The plant dies back to a hardy rootstock over winter and regrows vigorously each spring, tolerating shadier woodland conditions far better than annual buckwheat. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigorous leaf production and to share starts, since named forms rarely come true from self-sown seed.

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or potted runners in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich woodland soil; establishes quickly along stream banks, bog edges, or beneath dense canopy.

directions: Plant rooted divisions or potted runners in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich woodland soil in partial to full shade, siting it along stream banks, bog edges, or beneath dense tree canopy where little else will fruit. Dwarf raspberry spreads by trailing, mostly thornless stolons to knit together a soft groundcover only a few inches tall, and unlike upright raspberries it needs no staking or pruning to stay productive. Small, sparse-seeded red berries ripen in mid to late summer with a tart, juicy flavor best eaten fresh off the runners rather than harvested in quantity for preserves. Because it spreads indefinitely in favorable wet shade, give it a contained bed or a naturalized woodland corner where its running habit is an asset rather than a nuisance.
sources: native plant nursery listings (Hammarlund Nursery, Alcla Native Plants)
